content: Allergic colitis is a non-IgE-mediated immunological reaction to food protein antigens, most commonly cow's milk and soy proteins. The exact mechanism underlying this condition remains unknown, but it is believed to be mediated by T-cells. These activated T-cells recruit eosinophils and other polymorphonuclear cells into the intestinal tract, leading to inflammation and damage. In some cases, affected children may later develop specific IgE antibodies. Genetic predisposition may also play a role, as the condition is sometimes observed within families. The condition typically develops insidiously in early infancy and is most commonly triggered by an allergy to cow's milk protein. Between 20% and 40% of patients with allergic colitis also exhibit allergies to both cow's milk and soy proteins. Allergic colitis is generally benign and resolves completely in most children without long-term complications. The most common symptom is the passage of blood-streaked stool in an otherwise healthy infant. There are no specific laboratory findings pathognomonic for allergic colitis, but the presence of eosinophils in the stool, in conjunction with typical clinical findings, is suggestive of the diagnosis. A detailed history and physical examination are essential for diagnosis. Endoscopy with biopsy may be required in atypical cases to confirm the diagnosis. Gross endoscopic findings may include focal or diffuse erythema, friable and edematous mucosa, nodular hyperplasia, and/or ulcerations, often localized to the rectosigmoid area. Microscopic examination typically reveals preserved mucosal architecture with eosinophilic infiltrates. The prevalence of allergic colitis is not precisely known, but food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis (FPIAP) is the most common cause of non-infectious colitis in infancy. FPIAP has been reported in 16% to 64% of infants presenting with rectal bleeding. The condition is most commonly observed in exclusively breastfed infants, while food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) is more often associated with formula-fed infants. Differential diagnosis includes other causes of colitis and systemic diseases. In infants, allergic colitis must be distinguished from necrotizing enterocolitis, infectious colitis, anal fissures, intussusception, and volvulus. In adolescents and adults, it must be differentiated from inflammatory bowel disease, infectious colitis, and colorectal malignancy. The mainstay of treatment is dietary management, which includes allergen avoidance, treatment of severe allergic manifestations, and eventual reintroduction of the allergen into the diet. There is no indication for surgical intervention in allergic colitis. Spontaneous resolution may occur in approximately 20% of cases without elimination of the triggering food, and most infants will tolerate the offending food by 1 to 3 years of age. Screening for allergic colitis is not recommended, and there are no established methods for primary or secondary prevention. However, avoiding identified food allergens until tolerance is demonstrated is crucial.
